# Limiting Distribution of $U_n = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^2}$

## Setting Up the Problem

Since $Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(1)$ are i.i.d., I need to find the mean of $Y_i^2$ to apply the Law of Large Numbers.

## Computing $E[Y^2]$ for $Y \sim \text{Poisson}(1)$

Using the identity $Y^2 = Y(Y-1) + Y$:

$$E[Y^2] = E[Y(Y-1)] + E[Y] = \lambda + \lambda = 2\lambda$$

With $\lambda = 1$:

$$E[Y^2] = 2$$

## Applying the Strong Law of Large Numbers

Since $Y_i^2$ are i.i.d. with $E[Y^2] = 2 < \infty$, the SLLN gives:

$$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^2 \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} E[Y^2] = 2$$

## Applying the Continuous Mapping Theorem

The function $g(x) = \sqrt{x}$ is continuous at $x = 2 > 0$, so:

$$U_n = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^2} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} \sqrt{2}$$

## Conclusion

Since $U_n$ converges almost surely to the constant $\sqrt{2}$, the limiting distribution is a **degenerate (point-mass) distribution** at $\sqrt{2}$. Its CDF is:

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x < \sqrt{2} \\ 1, & x \geq \sqrt{2} \end{cases}$$

$$\boxed{\sqrt{2}}$$
